summary: This is a Naked Scientists forum thread (2010) asking why people remember names and other things once they stop trying to recall them. Forum members propose explanations: a subconscious process keeps searching, retrieval-induced forgetting and the recall of distant memories into easily accessible ones, memory compression for unused information, the role of sleep in reorganizing memory, and cue-based association in memory networks. The thread is mostly opinion and anecdote, with a few cited references.
one_line: A 2010 Naked Scientists forum thread discussing why forgotten names and memories suddenly return when people stop trying to recall them.
key_facts: The forum thread 'Why do you remember things when you stop trying to?' was started by user Geezer on 24/02/2010.
The opening post describes getting stuck trying to remember names, and the name suddenly popping into mind later when not trying to remember it.
RD replied that a subconscious subroutine keeps looking for the information until it finds it or a certain time period has elapsed, citing the Wikipedia article on 'User illusion'.
JnA suggested retrieval-induced forgetting as an explanation and linked a PubMed article (11082860).
Jessica H described a talk by a cognitive psychologist at Ohio Wesleyan University about college students who had taken Spanish in high school but not college.
In that experiment, students were tested on Spanish vocabulary and grammar, and when retested later they recalled more answers the second time.

Jessica H said the psychologist's model had two reservoirs of memories, one easily accessible and one distant, and that trying to recall a distant memory can shuffle it into the accessible reservoir, but it can take time.
Geezer proposed that the brain compresses unused information into an archive, so retrieval takes a long time because the brain must find and decompress it.
Chris (The Naked Scientist) said we don't stop thinking about something when we stop consciously paying attention to it, since unconscious processing continues.
Geezer asked whether sleep is essential to the brain reorganizing retained information, and suggested this might imply an upper limit to brain capacity.
Jessica H cited a Psychology Today article titled 'Sleep boosts memory' and said pulling all-nighters to study is a bad idea.
Geezer's upper limit idea was that increased brain capacity might require even more sleep, so humans may already be near a maximum practical brain size.
Jessica H suggested that physical constraints such as childbirth-related head size may be a bigger limit on brain size than sleep.
EatsRainbows suggested memory works through a network of associations where cues draw memories forth, and that focusing on the wrong cue may hinder recall.
